analysis_summary: Deep analysis of SVG Support v2.5.14. Plugin allows SVG uploads, inline rendering, and sanitization. Reviewed all entry points, AJAX handlers, REST API hooks, upload sanitization flow, meta registration, and SQL queries. Identified 1 confirmed finding (Stored XSS via SVG upload with sanitization bypass for privileged roles), 1 review-worthy issue (register_meta with __return_true auth_callback), and multiple false positives from Phase 1 anomalies. The plugin's core sanitization via enshrined/svg-sanitize library is sound for default configurations. The primary risk surface is the configurable sanitization bypass for admin-designated roles.

findings.vuln_type: Stored XSS via SVG Upload (Sanitization Bypass for Configured Roles)

reasoning.hypothesis: A user whose role is listed in the 'sanitize_on_upload_roles' plugin setting can upload an SVG file containing malicious JavaScript (e.g., <svg onload='alert(1)'> or <script> tags) that bypasses the enshrined/svg-sanitize sanitizer, because the sanitization step is conditionally skipped for those roles. The unsanitized SVG is stored on disk and served to other users, resulting in Stored XSS when the SVG is rendered inline or viewed directly.
reasoning.trace: 1. User uploads SVG via media uploader (wp_handle_upload_prefilter hook at attachment.php:400). 2. bodhi_svgs_sanitize_svg() is called (line 309). 3. File extension check passes (line 316). 4. Content validation passes for valid SVG with malicious payloads (lines 331-338). 5. MIME type check passes (line 341-344). 6. Nonce check passes for logged-in user (line 351). 7. At line 360, sanitize_on_upload_roles_array is loaded from plugin settings. 8. At line 365, array_intersect checks if user's roles overlap with bypass roles. 9. If $no_sanitize_needed is non-empty (user role is in bypass list), the sanitization block at lines 371-395 is SKIPPED. 10. File is returned unsanitized and stored in uploads directory. 11. When the SVG is viewed (directly via URL, or inlined via the plugin's JS replacement mechanism at enqueue.php:92-144), malicious JavaScript executes in the viewer's browser context.
reasoning.defenses: 1. The sanitize_on_upload_roles option defaults to an empty array (svg-support.php:131), meaning by default ALL uploads are sanitized. The bypass requires an admin to explicitly configure roles to skip sanitization. 2. The upload is restricted to roles in the 'restrict' setting (mime-types.php:36-37), defaulting to 'administrator' only. 3. The enshrined/svg-sanitize library is used for sanitization when active (lines 372-387). 4. For REST API uploads, bodhi_svgs_rest_pre_upload() at line 498 always force-sanitizes regardless of role, but bodhi_svgs_rest_insert_attachment() at line 527 re-applies the role-based bypass logic after insertion.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if sanitization bypass requires admin to configure it
refutation_attempts.result: Not refuted — admin must explicitly add roles to 'sanitize_on_upload_roles'. Default is empty array = sanitize everything. However, this is a prominent setting on the admin page (svgs-settings-page.php:114-136) and commonly configured by site admins who trust their editors/authors.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if WordPress core prevents serving SVG with script content
refutation_attempts.result: Not refuted — WordPress serves SVGs as image/svg+xml from the uploads directory. Browsers will execute JavaScript in SVGs served with this MIME type when navigated to directly or embedded via <object>/<embed>. The plugin's inline rendering (img-to-svg replacement via JS) also injects raw SVG into the DOM.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if the plugin's frontend sanitization (DOMPurify) mitigates this
refutation_attempts.result: Partially refuted — when 'sanitize_svg_front_end' is enabled (default: on) and advanced mode is active, DOMPurify.min.js is loaded (enqueue.php:82-85). However, this only protects the inline SVG replacement path, not direct SVG URL access. And DOMPurify is client-side JS, not server-side.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if REST API path also has the bypass
refutation_attempts.result: Not refuted — bodhi_svgs_rest_insert_attachment() at line 537 applies the same role-based bypass: if user's role is in sanitize_on_upload_roles_array, sanitization is skipped. However, bodhi_svgs_rest_pre_upload() at line 506 always calls bodhi_svgs_sanitize() which does sanitize. There's a double-sanitization flow for REST: pre-upload sanitizes, then rest_insert_attachment may re-sanitize. The pre-upload sanitization cannot be bypassed by role.

reasoning.conclusion: Confirmed Stored XSS. When an admin configures 'sanitize_on_upload_roles' to include a role (e.g., 'administrator' or 'editor'), users with that role can upload unsanitized SVG files containing JavaScript payloads. These are stored on disk and served to other users. The default configuration is safe (all uploads sanitized), but the feature explicitly enables this bypass. Severity is medium because: (1) requires admin configuration of the bypass, (2) attacker needs an account with upload_files capability AND a role in the bypass list, (3) impact is authenticated Stored XSS affecting other admin/editor users viewing the SVG.

findings.poc_description: 1. As admin, go to Settings > SVG Support. In 'Do not sanitize for these roles', add 'Editor'. 2. As an editor-role user, upload an SVG file containing: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><script>alert(document.cookie)</script></svg>. 3. The SVG is stored without sanitization. 4. When another user (e.g., admin) visits the direct SVG URL (e.g., /wp-content/uploads/2024/01/malicious.svg), JavaScript executes in their browser. 5. Alternatively, if inline rendering is enabled, the SVG content is injected into DOM on front-end pages, executing the script.
findings.remediation: Remove the role-based sanitization bypass entirely, or ensure sanitization is always applied regardless of user role. If the bypass is retained as a feature, add a prominent warning about the XSS implications and consider adding Content-Security-Policy headers for SVG files.

reasoning.hypothesis: The register_meta call with auth_callback => '__return_true' allows any authenticated user to update the 'inline_featured_image' meta field on posts they can edit via the REST API, bypassing role-specific authorization checks.
reasoning.trace: 1. bodhi_svgs_register_meta() is called on 'init' hook (line 90). 2. register_meta('post', 'inline_featured_image', ...) is called with 'show_in_rest' => true and 'auth_callback' => '__return_true' (lines 82-87). 3. When a REST API request updates a post's meta, WordPress checks: (a) can user edit the post (handled by REST controller), (b) can user edit this meta key (handled by auth_callback). 4. Since auth_callback is __return_true, step (b) always passes. 5. However, step (a) is enforced by WordPress core REST API — users must have edit_post capability for the specific post.
reasoning.defenses: WordPress REST API post endpoint enforces current_user_can('edit_post', $post_id) before processing meta updates. This means subscribers (who lack edit_posts capability) cannot exploit this. Only users who can already edit the post can modify this meta field.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if the REST API allows meta-only updates without edit_post capability
refutation_attempts.result: Refuted — WordPress REST API WP_REST_Posts_Controller::update_item_permissions_check() requires edit_post capability. Meta updates are part of the post update flow.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if there's a separate meta endpoint that bypasses post permissions
refutation_attempts.result: Refuted — WordPress does not expose a standalone meta update endpoint for post meta. Meta updates go through the post update endpoint.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if the meta field has security-relevant impact
refutation_attempts.result: Partially not refuted — the inline_featured_image meta only controls whether the featured image gets a CSS class for inline SVG rendering (featured-image.php:95-115). The impact is cosmetic/functional, not directly a security bypass.

reasoning.conclusion: The __return_true auth_callback is a best-practice violation but not exploitable in standard WordPress configurations due to the REST API's post-level permission checks. However, if a third-party plugin grants broader post editing capabilities (e.g., allowing subscribers to edit specific posts), this auth_callback would allow those users to modify this meta field without any additional authorization. The impact (toggling inline SVG rendering for featured images) is low severity. Marking as REVIEW because the pattern is insecure-by-design even if current impact is minimal.
reasoning.why_uncertain: Cannot determine if the target environment uses plugins that grant broader post-editing capabilities to lower-privileged roles.
reasoning.resolution_path: Test in an environment with plugins like 'Members' or 'User Role Editor' that grant subscribers edit_posts capability to confirm exploitability.

findings.poc_description: 1. With default WordPress roles, this is not exploitable. 2. If a subscriber were granted edit_posts capability via a third-party plugin, they could send: POST /wp-json/wp/v2/posts/{id} with body { 'meta': { 'inline_featured_image': true } } to toggle inline SVG rendering on any post they can edit. 3. Impact is limited to cosmetic changes (adds style-svg CSS class to featured image).
findings.remediation: Replace '__return_true' auth_callback with a proper capability check: 'auth_callback' => function($allowed, $meta_key, $post_id) { return current_user_can('edit_post', $post_id); }

findings.vuln_type: AJAX Handler Registered for Unauthenticated Users (Dead Code with nopriv Registration)
findings.auth_required: none (nopriv registration), but effectively author+ due to guards

reasoning.hypothesis: The AJAX handler bodhi_svgs_featured_image_inline_toggle is registered on wp_ajax_nopriv_ hook, making it accessible to unauthenticated users. If the nonce check or capability check can be bypassed, unauthenticated users could modify post meta.
reasoning.trace: 1. Handler registered at line 160: add_action('wp_ajax_nopriv_bodhi_svgs_featured_image_inline_toggle', ...). 2. Function at line 134 checks nonce with action 'svg-support-featured' (line 136). 3. wp_send_json_error() is called on nonce failure, which calls wp_die() — execution stops. 4. Capability check at line 140: current_user_can('edit_posts') — unauthenticated users always fail this. 5. No wp_create_nonce('svg-support-featured') exists anywhere in the plugin — the nonce is never generated. 6. No JavaScript code sends AJAX requests to this endpoint.
reasoning.defenses: 1. Nonce check at line 136 blocks all requests (nonce is never generated). 2. wp_send_json_error calls wp_die(), halting execution. 3. current_user_can('edit_posts') at line 140 would block unauthenticated users even if nonce passed. 4. This appears to be dead code — no frontend JS triggers this AJAX action.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if the nonce 'svg-support-featured' is generated anywhere
refutation_attempts.result: Refuted — grep across entire plugin finds no wp_create_nonce or wp_nonce_field with action 'svg-support-featured'. The handler can never receive a valid nonce.
Refuted — wp_send_json_error() calls wp_send_json() which calls wp_die(). Execution halts at line 137.

refutation_attempts.attempt: Check if there's an IDOR in the handler (post_id without ownership check)
refutation_attempts.result: Not refuted — line 140 uses current_user_can('edit_posts') not current_user_can('edit_post', $post_id). An Author could modify meta on any post, not just their own. However, the handler is dead code due to missing nonce generation.

reasoning.conclusion: The nopriv registration is a code quality issue, but the handler is effectively dead code because the nonce is never generated anywhere in the plugin. No legitimate request can reach the meta update logic. The IDOR (generic edit_posts check vs per-post edit_post check) exists in the code but is not exploitable because the handler cannot be invoked. Marking as REVIEW rather than TP because: (1) the handler is dead code, (2) if the nonce generation were added in a future version, the IDOR would become exploitable.
reasoning.why_uncertain: Future plugin versions might add nonce generation for this endpoint, activating the dead code path and exposing the IDOR.
reasoning.resolution_path: 1. Remove the wp_ajax_nopriv_ registration (line 160) since this is an admin action. 2. Replace current_user_can('edit_posts') with current_user_can('edit_post', $post_id) for proper per-post authorization. 3. Add nonce generation in the relevant admin JS/template if the handler is intended to be functional.

findings.poc_description: Not exploitable in current version — nonce is never generated. If nonce generation were added: 1. As an Author, obtain a valid nonce. 2. Send POST to admin-ajax.php?action=bodhi_svgs_featured_image_inline_toggle with nonce, post_id=(admin's post ID), checked=true. 3. The inline_featured_image meta would be set on the admin's post without ownership verification.
findings.remediation: 1. Remove wp_ajax_nopriv_ registration (line 160). 2. Change current_user_can('edit_posts') to current_user_can('edit_post', $post_id) at line 140. 3. Either implement nonce generation or remove the dead handler entirely.

negative_findings.analysis: Two $wpdb->query() calls at lines 10 and 24 use hardcoded meta_key='inline_featured_image' and meta_value comparisons. No user input enters these queries. The only dynamic values are $wpdb->postmeta which is the WordPress table prefix, not user-controlled. The function bodhi_svgs_cleanup_duplicate_meta() is only called from bodhi_svgs_version_updates() during admin_init when a version upgrade is detected (svg-support.php:103-106).
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If a future version passes user-controlled data into these queries.

negative_findings.analysis: The Phase 1 anomalies flagged missing nonce checks in admin_init handlers. Analysis of each: (1) bodhi_svgs_register_settings (admin-init.php:84-92) — calls register_setting() which is a WordPress registration API, not a state-changing operation triggered by user input. WordPress handles CSRF for settings forms via settings_fields() (svgs-settings-page.php:84). (2) bodhi_svgs_remove_old_sanitize_setting (admin-init.php:98-107) — reads from database, conditionally removes a deprecated option key. No user input. (3) bodhi_svgs_advanced_mode (admin-init.php:114-128) — reads from database, returns boolean. Pure read. (4) bodhi_svgs_display_thumbs (thumbnail-display.php:10-51) — output buffering for admin media library page, no state change. (5) bodhi_svgs_version_updates (svg-support.php:84-107) — version comparison and migration, no user input. None of these handlers process user-supplied data or perform state-changing operations that require CSRF protection.
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If any of these handlers are modified to accept and process user-supplied POST/GET data.

negative_findings.area: Missing Capability — admin_init handlers (anom_6 through anom_10)
negative_findings.analysis: Same handlers as above. (1) register_setting is a setup function, capability is enforced by WordPress when the settings form is submitted (manage_options required by the settings page via add_options_page at admin-init.php:14-20 and the explicit check at admin-init.php:35). (2-5) None of these handlers perform privilege-sensitive operations — they either read settings, perform one-time migrations, or set up output buffering for admin pages. The admin_init hook requires the user to be in wp-admin, which requires at minimum a subscriber-level login, but these handlers' operations are safe for any authenticated user.
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If any of these handlers are modified to perform admin-level operations (like updating settings) without capability checks.

negative_findings.analysis: Semgrep flagged line 99 of attachment.php. This line is: return (object) array( 'width' => $width, 'height' => $height ); inside bodhi_svgs_get_dimensions(). The $width and $height values come from simplexml_load_string parsing of SVG attributes (lines 94-96). These values are returned as an object and used in bodhi_svgs_response_for_svg() (line 34) to populate attachment metadata dimensions. They flow into wp_prepare_attachment_for_js response which is JSON-encoded by WordPress, not echoed raw. The values are also used in bodhi_svgs_generate_svg_attachment_metadata() where they are passed through intval() (lines 129-130). No raw output of these values occurs.
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If the dimension values are echoed directly in HTML context without escaping.

negative_findings.analysis: Multiple semgrep hits for loose comparison (==) instead of strict (===). All instances are comparing MIME types, option values, or version strings — not security-sensitive values like passwords, tokens, or hashes. Examples: $response['mime'] == 'image/svg+xml' (attachment.php:25), $bodhi_svgs_options['restrict'] == 'on' (svg-support.php:120). These loose comparisons are standard WordPress pattern for option comparison and pose no security risk. The semgrep rule name suggests hash/token/password comparison, but these are MIME type and option string comparisons.
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If any of these comparisons involve actual authentication tokens, passwords, or cryptographic values.

negative_findings.analysis: file_put_contents at line 390 writes sanitized SVG content back to the upload temp file during the wp_handle_upload_prefilter flow. The path comes from $file['tmp_name'] (line 312) which is controlled by PHP's upload handling, not user input. file_put_contents at line 555 in bodhi_svgs_rest_insert_attachment writes sanitized content back to the attachment file path from get_attached_file(), which returns the WordPress-managed upload path. Both write sanitized/clean content to paths controlled by WordPress, not user-supplied paths.
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If the file path derivation is changed to incorporate user-supplied data.

negative_findings.analysis: file_get_contents at lines 328, 375, and 550 read from upload temp files or WordPress-managed attachment paths. Line 328 reads $file_path = $file['tmp_name'] (PHP upload temp). Line 375 reads the same temp file for sanitization. Line 550 reads from get_attached_file() path. None of these paths are user-controlled strings — they are either PHP-managed temp paths or WordPress attachment paths.
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If the file path derivation includes user-controllable components.

negative_findings.analysis: All include/require calls use BODHI_SVGS_PLUGIN_PATH concatenated with hardcoded relative paths (e.g., 'admin/svgs-settings-page.php', 'vendor/autoload.php'). BODHI_SVGS_PLUGIN_PATH is set via plugin_dir_path(__FILE__) at svg-support.php:31, which returns the absolute path to the plugin directory. No user input enters any include path. The require_once at svg-support.php:104 uses BODHI_SVGS_PLUGIN_PATH . 'functions/meta-cleanup.php' — also hardcoded.
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If any include path incorporates user-supplied data.

negative_findings.analysis: The css_target option is stored via the settings form (admin-only, manage_options required). The sanitize callback at admin-init.php:55-57 applies esc_attr(sanitize_text_field()) on save. On output, it is consistently escaped: esc_attr() in enqueue.php:101-102, esc_attr() in attribute-control.php:37, and in featured-image.php:107 it is inserted into HTML via str_replace but only sets a CSS class name on an img tag. The save-time sanitization prevents injection of HTML special characters, and output-time escaping provides defense-in-depth.
negative_findings.reopening_condition: If the sanitize callback is removed or the output escaping is removed in a future version.

out_of_scope.reason: Third-party dependency. The sanitizer library itself is not the target of this review. Known CVEs in the library should be tracked separately.
Client-side JavaScript library. Bypass of client-side sanitization is always possible and is defense-in-depth, not a primary security control.

out_of_scope.area: WordPress core upload handling and REST API authentication
out_of_scope.reason: WordPress core security mechanisms (upload_files capability, REST API authentication, nonce system) are assumed to function correctly.
Multisite SVG upload configuration was reviewed at a light level. The function at mime-types.php:99-116 does not introduce additional attack surface beyond the standard upload flow.
